questions.title: Cold War — Truman Doctrine and the spread of communism in Europe, 1947

subQuestions.questionText: Study Source A (the cartoon). Identify TWO visual features in the cartoon that suggest the United States was opposed to the spread of communism in Europe. (Refer to Source A in the Addendum.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark each for any TWO of the following visual features (max 2):
Mark 1: Uncle Sam / USA figure positioned aggressively on one side of a dividing wall.
Mark 2: The 'Iron Curtain' wall or barrier dividing Europe into two halves.
Alternative: Dollar signs / Marshall Plan label showing US financial counter-strategy.
Alternative: Speech bubble / caption indicating US intent to fund European recovery (e.g. 'Europe MUST be rebuilt — or it falls to Communism!').
[Award 2 marks for any two valid features]
subQuestions.topic: Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the concept of containment as it relates to United States foreign policy after 1945.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Containment was the US foreign policy strategy of preventing the further spread of Soviet communism beyond areas where it already existed.
Mark 2: Developed by diplomat George Kennan and adopted by Truman — supporting countries at risk of communist takeover through economic and military aid.
[Award 2 marks for a clear explanation linking the concept to US policy after 1945]
subQuestions.topic: Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to Source B. What does President Truman mean when he says nations must choose 'between alternative ways of life'? Use evidence from the source to support your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2 (Explanation of meaning): Truman means nations must choose between democracy/capitalism on the one hand and communism/totalitarianism on the other — a binary choice between two opposing political systems with no middle ground (2 marks).
Marks 3–4 (Evidence from Source B): Reference to 'one way of life' based on 'the will of the majority… free elections, guarantees of individual liberty' (democracy) versus 'a minority forcibly imposed upon the majority… terror and oppression, a controlled press… fixed elections' (communism) (2 marks).
[Award 2 marks for explanation of meaning + 2 marks for source evidence]
subQuestions.topic: Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: How useful is Source A as evidence of American attitudes toward the Soviet Union in the late 1940s? Use the source and your own knowledge in your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 4 marks. Must reference source AND own knowledge for full marks.
USEFUL (1 mark each): Reflects actual US public opinion of the late 1940s; cartoons were widely read and shaped attitudes. Visual representation of the Iron Curtain metaphor (Churchill, 1946) shows the concept had entered popular culture.
LIMITATION (1 mark each): Represents only one American perspective — cartoons are inherently partisan. Does not capture Soviet or European perspectives on the Marshall Plan.
OWN KNOWLEDGE (1 mark): Marshall Plan offered $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe; Soviets rejected it as economic imperialism.
[Award 4 marks for a balanced answer combining source analysis and own knowledge]
subQuestions.topic: Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: Identify ONE similarity and ONE difference between the views expressed in Source A and Source B regarding the threat posed by communism.
subQuestions.memoText:
SIMILARITY (2 marks): Both portray communism as a threatening, aggressive system that endangers freedom / both support the USA taking a strong role in opposing it.
DIFFERENCE (2 marks): Source A uses a visual/satirical form and focuses on economic aid (Marshall Plan); Source B is a formal policy speech focusing on political ideology and moral duty.
[Award 2 marks for similarity + 2 marks for difference]
subQuestions.topic: Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: Assess the reliability of Source B as evidence of American intentions during the early Cold War period. In your answer, consider the origin, purpose, and possible bias of the source.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (ORIGIN): Truman is the sitting US President — primary source; but he is also the chief architect of the policy, so he has a strong motive to justify it.
Mark 2 (PURPOSE): Address to Congress — designed to persuade legislators to approve aid and commit to containment policy.
Mark 3 (BIAS): Portrays communism entirely negatively; ignores US economic interests in Europe's recovery and the fact that some communist parties had popular support.
Mark 4 (EVALUATION): Despite bias, reflects genuine US policymaking beliefs of the era; useful as evidence of Cold War rhetoric even if not fully objective.
[Award 4 marks for full coverage of origin, purpose, bias and overall evaluation]
subQuestions.topic: Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: 'The Truman Doctrine permanently divided Europe into two rival spheres of influence.' Using the evidence of BOTH sources AND your own knowledge, write a paragraph of 8–10 lines arguing whether you agree or disagree with this statement.
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Level 1–4 holistic rubric:
Level 4 (7–8 marks): Clear argument stated; both sources used with specific quotation; relevant own knowledge integrated; counter-argument acknowledged; conclusion answers question directly.
Level 3 (5–6 marks): Argument present; both sources referenced; some own knowledge; limited counter-argument.
Level 2 (3–4 marks): Some evidence from sources; limited own knowledge; argument weak or implied.
Level 1 (1–2 marks): Mostly descriptive; limited or no source reference; no clear argument.

Key content for full marks:
• AGREE: Truman Doctrine (1947) explicitly framed the world in binary terms; NATO formed 1949; Warsaw Pact 1955 — institutional division of Europe.
• AGREE: Marshall Plan (Source A) deepened Western dependence on US; Soviets refused and set up Comecon — economic division followed ideological division.
• Source B evidence: Truman's language ('two ways of life') made compromise politically impossible.
• COUNTER: Division pre-existed the Doctrine — Soviet occupation of Eastern Europe began 1944–45; Churchill's Iron Curtain speech was March 1946.
• COUNTER: The division was already 'permanent' before 1947 — Truman merely formalised and funded it.
• Conclusion must directly state whether the candidate agrees/disagrees and why, using source evidence.
subQuestions.topic: Cold War

questions.title: Angola — Foreign powers and Cold War intervention, 1975–1976

subQuestions.questionText: Study Source A (the cartoon). Name TWO foreign powers depicted as intervening in Angola in 1975. (Refer to Source A in the Addendum.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award any TWO of the following (1 mark each, max 2):
Mark 1: USA / CIA / United States.
Mark 2: USSR / Soviet Union.
Alternative: Cuba.
Alternative: South Africa / SADF.
[Award 2 marks for any two correctly named foreign powers]
subQuestions.topic: Independent Africa — Angola and Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why Angola became a Cold War battleground in 1975. Use your own knowledge.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Portugal granted independence to Angola in November 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (1974), creating a power vacuum.
Mark 2: Three movements competed: MPLA (Marxist, backed by USSR/Cuba), FNLA (backed by USA/China), UNITA (backed by USA/South Africa).
Mark 3: Cold War logic — USA feared a Marxist state in Southern Africa would spread communism and threaten Western mineral interests.
Mark 4: South Africa feared an MPLA government would support SWAPO and ANC insurgents operating from Angolan territory.
[Award 4 marks for any four valid reasons demonstrating Cold War context]
subQuestions.topic: Independent Africa — Angola and Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to Source B. According to this source, why did Cuba intervene in Angola? Use evidence from the source in your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Cuba framed its intervention as anti-imperialist solidarity, not aggression — 'Cuba's intervention in Angola was not aggression — it was solidarity.'
Mark 2: South African armoured columns were advancing northward from Namibia and threatened to destroy the MPLA government.
Mark 3: Humanitarian/solidarity framing — 'Cuba sent soldiers, doctors, and teachers — not settlers or exploiters.'
Mark 4: USA funded FNLA and UNITA forces — Cuba presented itself as a counterweight to imperialist intervention.
[Award 4 marks for clear use of source evidence to explain Cuba's stated motives]
subQuestions.topic: Independent Africa — Angola and Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: How reliable is Source B as evidence of Cuba's motives for intervening in Angola? Consider the origin and purpose of the source.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (ORIGIN): Cuban Ministry of Defence communiqué — official government document; primary source but heavily propagandistic.
Mark 2 (PURPOSE): Justify Cuban intervention domestically and internationally; portray Cuba as liberator not aggressor.
Mark 3 (BIAS): Ignores Soviet direction of Cuban involvement; overstates solidarity motivation versus Cold War strategic gain.
Mark 4 (EVALUATION): Despite limitations, Cuba did send 36 000+ troops and did halt the South African advance — factually verifiable core.
[Award 4 marks for a balanced reliability assessment covering origin, purpose, bias and evaluation]
subQuestions.topic: Independent Africa — Angola and Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: Study Source A. Explain the message communicated by the cartoonist about the situation in Angola in 1975. Refer to at least TWO visual elements in your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2 (Message): Angola was treated as a Cold War battlefield by outside powers rather than allowed to determine its own future (2 marks).
Mark 3 (Visual element 1): Multiple large arrows from different countries pointing inward at a small Angola — suggesting overwhelming foreign interference.
Mark 4 (Visual element 2): Labels identifying USA, USSR, Cuba, South Africa — showing how many external actors were involved simultaneously.
[Award 2 marks for the message + 1 mark for each visual element referenced]
subQuestions.topic: Independent Africa — Angola and Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: To what extent do Sources A and B agree about the nature of foreign involvement in Angola? Quote evidence from BOTH sources.
subQuestions.memoText:
AGREE (2 marks): Both acknowledge multiple foreign powers intervening — Source A shows arrows from four countries; Source B names USA, South Africa, Cuba and (by implication) USSR.
DIFFER (2 marks): Source A presents all intervention as equally problematic ('Scramble for Angola'); Source B portrays Cuban/Soviet intervention as justified solidarity and USA/South Africa as imperialist aggression.
[Award 2 marks for agreement + 2 marks for difference, with quoted evidence from BOTH sources]
subQuestions.topic: Independent Africa — Angola and Cold War

subQuestions.questionText: 'Foreign interference in Angola in 1975 made a peaceful transition to independence impossible.' Using BOTH sources AND your own knowledge, write a paragraph of 8–10 lines arguing FOR or AGAINST this statement.
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Level 1–4 holistic rubric (same as Q1.7):
Level 4 (7–8): Clear argument; both sources quoted; own knowledge integrated; counter-argument acknowledged; direct conclusion.
Level 3 (5–6): Argument present; both sources referenced; some own knowledge.
Level 2 (3–4): Some source evidence; limited own knowledge; weak argument.
Level 1 (1–2): Mostly descriptive; little or no source reference.

Key content for full marks:
• AGREE: Three movements (MPLA, FNLA, UNITA) became proxies for superpowers — internal political settlement was impossible when each faction had a superpower sponsor.
• AGREE: South African military invasion in November 1975 escalated military conflict beyond what Angolans alone could have managed.
• AGREE: CIA spent $32 million supporting FNLA/UNITA; Soviet/Cuban support meant the MPLA did not need to compromise.
• COUNTER: The three movements were already in violent conflict before significant foreign intervention (pre-1975).
• COUNTER: Portugal's abrupt withdrawal without a transition plan was equally, if not more, destabilising.
subQuestions.topic: Independent Africa — Angola and Cold War

questions.title: Civil Rights — Birmingham Children's Crusade, Alabama, May 1963

subQuestions.questionText: Study Source A (the photograph). Describe what is happening in this image. Identify at least TWO details visible in the photograph. (Refer to Source A in the Addendum.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award any TWO accurate visual observations (1 mark each, max 2):
Mark 1: Children/young people marching in a street or public space.
Mark 2: Police officers using high-pressure water hoses against the marchers.
Alternative: Protesters carrying signs/banners with civil rights slogans (e.g. 'We Shall Overcome').
[Award 2 marks for any two valid observations]
subQuestions.topic: Civil Society Protests — Civil Rights Movement (USA)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why the Birmingham campaign of 1963 was considered a turning point in the American Civil Rights Movement.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Deliberate strategic choice — SCLC/MLK chose Birmingham as one of the most segregated cities in the South, with Bull Connor as Commissioner of Public Safety, whose brutality was predictable.
Mark 2: Children's Crusade — use of school-age children who could march while adults worked ensured mass numbers and media sympathy.
Mark 3: Television coverage of police violence shocked national and international audiences, generating enormous political pressure.
Mark 4: Led directly to Kennedy's civil rights address (June 1963) and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 — turning point toward legislative change.
[Award 4 marks for any four valid points with clear historical reasoning]
subQuestions.topic: Civil Society Protests — Civil Rights Movement (USA)

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to Source B. What does Shuttlesworth mean when he says 'Birmingham has shown the world the face of American apartheid'? Use evidence from the source.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2 (Meaning): Shuttlesworth compares American racial segregation to South African apartheid — arguing that despite the USA's claims to democracy, its racial oppression was equally systematic and visible (2 marks).
Marks 3–4 (Source evidence): 'Every image of a child knocked to the ground by a water cannon is a picture that tells the world what segregation truly means' — the violence exposed the hypocrisy of US democratic claims (2 marks).
[Award 2 marks for explanation + 2 marks for source evidence]
subQuestions.topic: Civil Society Protests — Civil Rights Movement (USA)

subQuestions.questionText: What are the limitations of Source A as evidence of the impact of the Birmingham campaign? Consider who took it, when, and what it can and cannot tell us.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: A single photograph captures only one moment — cannot convey the full 6-week campaign or the broader pattern of violence and protest.
Mark 2: The photographer (Bill Hudson, AP) chose what to frame — other events happening simultaneously are excluded.
Mark 3: Does not tell us about the outcome of the protest, the marchers' experience, or the legal/political response.
Mark 4: Black-and-white medium (historical) may reduce emotional immediacy compared to colour; but iconic power should be acknowledged.
[Award 4 marks for a thoughtful evaluation of the source's limitations]
subQuestions.topic: Civil Society Protests — Civil Rights Movement (USA)

subQuestions.questionText: How useful is Source B in helping us understand the goals of the Civil Rights Movement in 1963? Refer to the source and your own knowledge.
subQuestions.memoText:
USEFUL (Marks 1–2):
Mark 1: Shuttlesworth was a key Birmingham SCLC leader — primary source from a direct participant revealing movement goals.
Mark 2: Explicitly states goals — federal action, end to segregation, recognition of dignity ('we will not accept a system that treats us as less than human').
LIMITATION (Marks 3–4):
Mark 3: Written as a press statement — designed to persuade; may overstate unity and courage, understate internal divisions.
Mark 4: Represents leadership perspective only — does not capture views of ordinary marchers or those who opposed the children's march strategy.
[Award 4 marks for balanced usefulness analysis combining source and own knowledge]
subQuestions.topic: Civil Society Protests — Civil Rights Movement (USA)

subQuestions.questionText: Do Sources A and B support each other as evidence of the brutal treatment of civil rights protesters in Birmingham? Quote evidence from BOTH sources.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2 (Brutality of police response): Both sources confirm the brutal police response — Source A shows hoses directed at marchers; Source B states 'they marched knowing they would face fire hoses and police dogs' (2 marks).
Marks 3–4 (Defiance despite violence): Both show defiance continuing despite violence — Source A shows marchers still standing; Source B states 'We will not stop. We will not retreat.' (2 marks).
[Award 4 marks for two clear points of agreement, each with quoted evidence from BOTH sources]
subQuestions.topic: Civil Society Protests — Civil Rights Movement (USA)

subQuestions.questionText: 'The Birmingham Children's Crusade of 1963 forced the federal government to take meaningful action on civil rights.' Using BOTH sources AND your own knowledge, write a paragraph of 8–10 lines arguing whether you agree or disagree.
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Level 1–4 holistic rubric (same as Q1.7).
Level 4 (7–8): Clear argument; both sources used with specific quotation; relevant own knowledge; counter-argument acknowledged; direct conclusion.
Level 3 (5–6): Argument present; both sources referenced; some own knowledge.
Level 2 (3–4): Some source evidence; limited own knowledge.
Level 1 (1–2): Mostly descriptive; little or no source reference.

Key content for full marks:
• AGREE: Kennedy watched footage of children being knocked over by water hoses — called it 'shameful' and announced civil rights legislation in June 1963.
• AGREE: The Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965) were legislative outcomes traceable to Birmingham's media impact.
• Source A: visible proof of state violence against children — impossible for federal government to ignore internationally.
• Source B: Shuttlesworth explicitly calls on Kennedy to act — shows the movement was strategically demanding federal intervention.
• COUNTER: Kennedy was cautious and slow; Birmingham alone did not produce immediate action — JFK's assassination (November 1963) and Johnson's political skill were also crucial factors.
• COUNTER: Executive orders and court decisions predated Birmingham (Brown v Board 1954; Little Rock 1957).
subQuestions.topic: Civil Society Protests — Civil Rights Movement (USA)

subQuestions.questionText: 'The United States lost the Vietnam War not because of superior North Vietnamese military strength, but because of flawed strategy and domestic opposition at home.' Critically discuss. (Approximately 400–500 words.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Section B essay rubric (each criterion out of 10):
• Argument / Stance (10): Clear thesis in introduction; consistent argument throughout; conclusion directly answers question.
• Evidence (10): Accurate, specific, and relevant historical facts; variety of examples; no irrelevant content.
• Analysis / Evaluation (10): Evidence linked to argument; multiple perspectives; acknowledges complexity.
• Structure (10): Clear intro–body–conclusion; logical paragraph sequencing; transitions between ideas.
• Conclusion (10): Directly answers the question; synthesises argument; does not merely repeat introduction.

Key content (candidate must take a clear stance and substantiate):
• AGREE: US tactics (search-and-destroy, strategic hamlets, napalm, defoliation) alienated Vietnamese civilians and failed to eliminate guerrillas permanently.
• AGREE: Tet Offensive 1968 — military setback for the NLF but psychological catastrophe for US credibility; Walter Cronkite broadcast turned public opinion.
• AGREE: Anti-war movement — Kent State (1970), Vietnam Veterans Against the War, Congressional opposition.
• AGREE: Pentagon Papers (1971) revealed government deception; the credibility gap destroyed public trust.
• COUNTER: Viet Cong/NVA demonstrated exceptional military capability — tunnels, supply lines (Ho Chi Minh Trail), guerrilla tactics defeated a conventional army.
• COUNTER: NV willingness to absorb massive casualties was itself a form of military strength.
• Good essays will argue the relative weight of factors — not just list them.
subQuestions.topic: Vietnam War — End of the Cold War and a New World Order

subQuestions.questionText: To what extent was the use of guerrilla warfare by the Viet Cong the decisive factor in America's defeat in Vietnam? Substantiate your answer with relevant evidence. (Approximately 400–500 words.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Section B essay rubric (Argument 10 / Evidence 10 / Analysis 10 / Structure 10 / Conclusion 10).

Key content (candidate must weigh guerrilla warfare against other factors):
• FOR: Tunnel systems, booby traps, and use of jungle terrain made conventional US tactics ineffective.
• FOR: Ability to fade into civilian population made the enemy impossible to distinguish — moral and tactical problem.
• FOR: Ho Chi Minh Trail supplied southern operations despite massive US bombing.
• COUNTER: Domestic US opposition was arguably more decisive — politicians could not sustain a war the public rejected.
• COUNTER: Cold War détente (Nixon/Kissinger) changed the strategic calculus; Gulf of Tonkin lies undermined political will.
• Best essays will weigh guerrilla warfare alongside political, strategic and domestic factors and arrive at a substantiated judgement.
subQuestions.topic: Vietnam War — End of the Cold War and a New World Order

subQuestions.questionText: 'Patrice Lumumba's removal from power in 1960 was primarily the result of Cold War interference rather than domestic political failure.' Do you agree? Motivate your answer. (Approximately 400–500 words.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Section B essay rubric (Argument 10 / Evidence 10 / Analysis 10 / Structure 10 / Conclusion 10).

Key content (candidate must take a clear position and substantiate):
• FOR COLD WAR: CIA authorised an assassination plot (Operation WIZARD); Eisenhower administration feared Lumumba's socialist leanings.
• FOR COLD WAR: Belgian technical personnel sabotaged Congolese government function after independence; Belgium funded Katangan secession under Tshombe.
• FOR COLD WAR: UN force (ONUC) sent but neutralised Lumumba by not acting against Mobutu's coup — Western direction of UN policy.
• COUNTER (DOMESTIC): Lumumba made political errors — alienating Kasavubu (his own president), failing to build coalitions, requesting Soviet aid which alarmed Western powers.
• COUNTER (DOMESTIC): His rhetorical style and rapid moves created domestic enemies — Mobutu's coup had Congolese participants, not just foreign direction.
• Balance required: Cold War interference was decisive, but Lumumba's domestic political failures created the conditions for it.
subQuestions.topic: Independent Africa — The Congo Crisis

subQuestions.questionText: To what extent did Mobutu's leadership of the Congo (Zaire) benefit ordinary Congolese citizens? Use relevant evidence to support your argument. (Approximately 400–500 words.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Section B essay rubric (Argument 10 / Evidence 10 / Analysis 10 / Structure 10 / Conclusion 10).

Key content:
• LIMITED BENEFIT: Early economic nationalisation of mining (GECAMINES) initially increased state revenue; brief period of infrastructure investment.
• HARM: Mobutuism / authenticity programme stripped Westernisation but replaced it with a personality cult; renamed country Zaire.
• HARM: Systematic kleptocracy — Mobutu accumulated a personal fortune of approximately $5 billion while national infrastructure collapsed.
• HARM: Political repression — opponents imprisoned, tortured, executed; no free press, no opposition parties.
• HARM: Economy collapsed — GDP fell, inflation rampant, copper/cobalt revenues siphoned off.
• Conclusion: Mobutu's rule benefited him and a small elite; ordinary Congolese experienced poverty, fear, and declining services.
subQuestions.topic: Independent Africa — The Congo Crisis

subQuestions.questionText: 'The Black Power Movement of the 1960s and 1970s did more to advance African American dignity and identity than it did to achieve political equality.' Critically discuss this view. (Approximately 400–500 words.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Section B essay rubric (Argument 10 / Evidence 10 / Analysis 10 / Structure 10 / Conclusion 10).

Key content:
• DIGNITY/IDENTITY: 'Black is Beautiful' movement; Afrocentric dress, hair, and culture reclaimed; rejection of the assimilation model.
• DIGNITY: SNCC's shift under Stokely Carmichael (1966) — Black Power speech in Mississippi; psychological liberation as a goal.
• POLITICAL LIMITS: Black Power's confrontational image gave opponents ammunition; the FBI's COINTELPRO targeted Black Panther Party leadership (Hampton killed 1969).
• POLITICAL LIMITS: Voter registration and legal desegregation (1964, 1965 Acts) were achieved by the mainstream Civil Rights Movement, not Black Power.
• COUNTER: Black Power did achieve some political goals — Black elected officials increased dramatically in the 1970s; community control of schools in some cities.
• Best essays will argue that dignity and political equality are not mutually exclusive — Black Power advanced both, but more visibly in the cultural sphere.
subQuestions.topic: Civil Society Protests — Black Power Movement (USA)

subQuestions.questionText: To what extent was the Black Panther Party a response to the failures of the mainstream Civil Rights Movement to address economic inequality and police brutality? Substantiate your answer. (Approximately 400–500 words.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Section B essay rubric (Argument 10 / Evidence 10 / Analysis 10 / Structure 10 / Conclusion 10).

Key content:
• FOR: Civil Rights Acts did not address economic inequality — the BPP's 10-Point Program explicitly targeted unemployment, housing and education.
• FOR: Police brutality continued after legal desegregation — BPP's armed patrols of police in Oakland were a direct response.
• FOR: Mainstream movement focused on the South; BPP based in Northern cities (Oakland, Chicago, New York) where formal segregation did not exist but poverty and police violence did.
• FOR: Free Breakfast for Children programme, health clinics — community self-sufficiency because federal programmes failed.
• COUNTER: BPP was also influenced by Malcolm X, Fanon and socialist internationalism — not purely reactive to mainstream Civil Rights.
• COUNTER: Some mainstream movement leaders (especially SNCC's later period) overlapped with Black Power — not a clean break.
subQuestions.topic: Civil Society Protests — Black Power Movement (USA)
